title: Hosted API demo: chat/text generation basics
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked BlueOak Labs through the Hosted API for chat/text generation: streaming responses, key params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p, stop), retries and idempotency, and the Console basics. BlueOak is evaluating hosted vs Dedicated for a consumer-facing chat assistant; main concerns are latency, cost, and PII handling. Next steps: send pricing, SOC2/security docs, and schedule an SE-led benchmark on their prompt set.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-08
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE); Liam Chen (Redwood SE); Maya Rodriguez (BlueOak CTO); Alex Kim (BlueOak ML Eng); Evan Stone (BlueOak Product)

[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Maya (BlueOak): Hey, Maya here.
[00:08] Alex: Alex here.
[00:10] Evan: Evan here.
[00:12] Sofia: Great. Quick agenda: show Hosted API chat/text basics, streaming, params, retries, and a quick look at Console and Optimize recommendations. Liam will jump into the demo.

[00:35] Liam (Redwood SE): Cool. So high level, Hosted API gives you simple REST/SDK for chat and text generation. We'll demo streaming which is useful for UX like progressive tokens. I'll share my screen now — sorry if the audio picks up.

[01:02] Liam: Starting with a simple chat call, here's the request body. We include model, messages, and params like temperature and max_tokens. Note the streaming flag — with streaming we send chunked token diffs over a SSE-style stream so frontend can render token-by-token.

[01:45] Alex (BlueOak): Can streaming help with perceived latency? Our product needs near real-time replies for a customer-facing assistant.

[01:52] Liam: Yes, exactly — perceived latency improves because tokens arrive incrementally. Actual time to first token is similar but UX feels faster. We also show how to set stop sequences to end generation early.

[02:25] Maya: What's the difference between your streaming and, ah, the one from, say, OpenAI? Any weird gotchas?

[02:33] Liam: Implementation is similar conceptually. One note: sometimes transcripts or names are mis-typed — in our logs you may see 'Redwood Dedicated' labeled wrong by auto-transcribe but runtime behavior is the same. For gotchas — handle reconnects and de-duplication on the client side because you may get partial last-chunk on network glitches.

[03:05] Evan: On reconnects, how do we avoid duplicate tokens?

[03:10] Liam: Good question. Use idempotency keys for non-streamed calls and a client-side token cursor for streams. For REST calls we recommend an idempotency key header for retries; our SDKs provide helpers to set that. For streaming, you can resume from the last confirmed token index — we expose chunk sequence metadata. Note: sequence metadata sometimes shows up as seq_num in logs; it's safe to treat it as advisory because of transcription labeling inside the UI.

[04:02] Alex: If we have bursty traffic, what happens? Are there rate limits?

[04:09] Sofia: Hosted API has rate limits and quotas. We'll include the quota table in the pricing packet. For production we'd recommend either Dedicated if you want guaranteed throughput, or Hosted with reserved bursts and configured throttling.

[04:28] Maya: Latency vs cost tradeoff — any guidance?

[04:32] Liam: Yes. Key levers: model size and quantization, batch size (server-side batching we do automatically), and caching. For latency-critical endpoints use smaller model variant or a lower-latency profile. Optimize suggests quantization and batching settings per workload — we'll show some recommendations in the Console.

[05:10] Evan: Can you show an example of parameter tuning?

[05:14] Liam: Sure. Example: lowering temperature reduces variance; lowering max_tokens reduces token cost and latency. top_p controls nucleus sampling; often set to 0.9 for creative tasks. Stop sequences can truncate early. See snippet: temperature:0.2, max_tokens:60, top_p:0.95.

[06:05] Alex: How about retries/backoff behaviour? If we hit a 5xx what should we do?

[06:11] Liam: Standard pattern: exponential backoff with jitter, max 3 fast retries for transient errors. For idempotent generation, include idempotency key; for streaming we recommend failing fast and prompting the client to re-request with resume logic. We'll share our SDK retry policy in the docs.

[06:50] Maya: Data handling: we can't send PII to any hosted vendor without scoping. Does Redwood persist request/response content?

[06:59] Sofia: We have configurable retention. Hosted by default retains short-term for debugging but enterprise customers can opt out or use Private/Dedicated with day-zero retention and VPC egress. We'll attach SOC 2 and data retention docs.

[07:30] Alex: Are there encryption/KMS options?

[07:33] Liam: Yes — KMS for key management for Dedicated/Private. For Hosted we integrate with cloud KMS and provide encryption at rest and in transit. We'll send the security pack.

[08:05] Evan: Walk me through a sample stream response?

[08:09] Liam: (shows console) You see connection open lines, then data: {"delta":"Hello","seq":1}, then subsequent deltas. On the Console request inspector we show per-request token counts, latency percentiles, and cost estimate.

[09:00] Maya: Is cost shown per-token?

[09:02] Sofia: Yes, tokenized cost and estimated unit price show up in Console. Optimize will also suggest where you can save costs by quantizing or changing model variant.

[09:28] Alex: How much effort to integrate the SDK? We have a node/React stack.

[09:32] Sofia: We offer Node and Python SDKs. Integration is basically installing the SDK, wiring API key, and using the chat client. We have quickstart repos I can share.

[10:05] Liam: Also show the technique for streaming in the browser: use EventSource or WebSocket proxy to hide API keys — don't embed keys in client. Best practice is to route through your backend and do short-lived tokens to the front end.

[11:00] Evan: We plan to run a 2-week POC. What would you recommend as a minimal success criteria?

[11:06] Sofia: Typical success criteria: 1) Latency to first token under X ms (we'll calibrate), 2) Acceptable quality as judged by sample prompts (>85% good), and 3) Cost per session within budget. Also security checklist completed.

[11:45] Maya: Would Dedicated make sense for us if we have 5000 concurrent users?

[11:50] Liam: Possibly — Dedicated gives reserved GPUs and predictable throughput. We'll need your traffic profile; if you have spiky peaks, Dedicated plus burst pools is good. For smaller scale Hosted with reserved capacity can work. We'll size it in the benchmark.

[12:20] Alex: Can we run a benchmark on a small GPU cluster to compare Redwood hosted vs our baseline?

[12:26] Liam: Yes — we'll run a SE-led benchmark with your prompt set. We'll simulate traffic and provide latency/cost numbers. Targeting 4/13 for the session.

[12:40] Sofia: Quick Console demo: here's the per-route dashboard, token cost, and traces. You can pin a model version and roll out canary. Also Optimize tab suggests quantization and batching profiles.

[13:25] Evan: Any known limitations with stop tokens or structured output?

[13:29] Liam: Structured output supported via JSON schema hints and function calling; stop tokens are advisory for streaming but reliable for most seq tasks. Edge case: extremely long stop sequences can cause tokenization mismatches — we document heuristics.

[14:05] Maya: Regarding retries, does Redwood expose retry-after header for throttled responses?

[14:11] Liam: Yes we return standard headers on rate limits; SDK will surface that. For heavy consumers we can negotiate quota or recommend Dedicated.

[14:40] Alex: What about observability hooks? Can we log traces to our instruments?

[14:46] Sofia: We provide tracing hooks, request ids, and exportable CSVs for cost/latency. We also have per-token trace for expensive calls — you can route them to your SIEM.

[15:10] Evan: Are there sample config suggestions for cost/latency?

[15:14] Liam: Yes. For chat assistants: temperature 0.2, max_tokens 60, top_p 0.9, enable prefix caching for repeated prompts, and set streaming for UX. Optimize will flag obvious wins like quantization or switching to a faster variant.

[16:00] Maya: Sounds good. Any blockers on our side to start a POC?

[16:05] Sofia: We just need sample prompts, expected concurrent sessions, and network access for the benchmark. We'll send pricing and security docs; after you sign the pilot TOS we can provision trial keys.

[16:30] Evan: Perfect. Please send everything to evan@blueoak.com.

[16:34] Sofia: Will do. Quick recap of next steps: send pricing and quickstart, attach SOC2 pack, schedule benchmark.

[16:45] Alex: One more small question: log retention windows on hosted by default?

[16:50] Liam: Default short-term 30 days; enterprise can configure retention or opt for no retention in Private/Dedicated.

[17:05] Maya: OK thanks everyone. Appreciate the demo.

[17:10] Sofia: Thanks all. We'll follow up with docs and calendar invite for benchmark.

[17:20] (meeting ends)
